title: Orchestration bounce scenario notes
content:
Summary:

Short notes from on-call and follow-up debugging for a recurring "bounce"/capacity-thrash pattern in the Dedicated GPU pool over the last 2 weeks. This doc captures commands I ran, raw snippets, heuristic checks, and hypotheses to hand off to SRE and scheduler owners. Not a finished postmortem — more a breadcrumb map for next investigators.

Context / symptom:
- Customer-facing latency spikes and 503s when a large batch of steady-state jobs (fair-share) overlapped with a sudden influx of short, high-priority requests.
- Pool appears to allocate new nodes, then evicts warm pods repeatedly (short-lived warmups that never reach full priming).
- Observed ≈3–7 minute cycles where available_capacity goes from 0 -> nominal -> 0 again, correlated with high churn and GPU warmup failures.

Timeline (rough):
- 2026-02-01 02:17 UTC: first alert from route latency SLO; host-scale-up triggered by scheduler policy.
- 2026-02-01 02:19 UTC: new nodes come up (k8s Ready), but many served requests still 503.
- 02:21–02:25 UTC: dozens of pods report "priming timeout" and are evicted (kube-eviction events + scheduler preemption logs).
- 02:28 UTC: autoscaler removes nodes after failed warmup; capacity drops.
- Pattern repeated with ~4–6 minute period for ~30 minutes.

Signals and dashboards I checked:
- Prometheus metrics: pool_total_gpus, pool_allocated_gpus, pool_ready_pods, pod_warm_success_rate (custom), model_kv_cache_miss_rate.
- Logs: kubelet, node-exporter GPU stats (nvidia-smi), serving-runtime agent (priming handshake logs).
- Console traces: per-route cost/latency + rollout trace that shows many fallbacks to smaller models.

Commands I ran (copyable):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=dedicated-a -n infra
- kubectl get pods -n dedicated-pools -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n dedicated-pools  # looked for readiness probe failures + eviction reasons
- kubectl logs <pod> -n dedicated-pools --previous  # check pre-eviction logs
- kubectl exec -it <pod> -n dedicated-pools -- /bin/bash -c "curl -s localhost:9100/metrics | grep warm"
- ssh node (g4-*) sudo journalctl -u serving-agent -f --no-pager
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 2
- curl -s 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=pod_warm_success_rate%7Bpool%3D%22dedicated-a%22%7D' | jq .

Representative error snippets collected:
- serving-agent: priming handshake failed: timeout_wait_for_kv_cache (t=30s)
- scheduler: insufficient resources: requested=1gpus allocatable=0 (after node-add)
- kubelet: eviction signal: nodefs.available below threshold, pod <name> evicted
- model-loader: failed to mmap quantized-weight.bin: invalid argument (file truncated?)

What surprised me / anomalies: 
- New nodes report GPU present and drivers OK (nvidia-smi shows GPU healthy), but serving-agent log shows repeated "KV init retries" and then timeout.
- Some pods never hit Ready even though containers are running; readiness probe timeout was the priming-check (waiting for full KV warm).
- Evicted pods sometimes show different eviction reasons (OOM vs disk pressure vs preemption) — suspicious that multiple eviction paths are contributing to churn rather than a single root cause.
- The autoscaler seemed conservative: it removed the node soon after pods failed, even when there were pending requests queued. Possible policy misread of warm failures as node unrecoverable.

Quick experiments attempted and outcomes: 
1) Increase priming timeout locally on a test shadow pool (increase from 30s -> 90s)
   - Result: warm success rate improved for large models but average tail latency for first-token increased for some routes (expected). Churn reduced but not eliminated.
2) Disable aggressive node removal in autoscaler (set scaleDownUnneededTime=6m -> 12m) on canary pool
   - Result: fewer node removes observed, but cluster cost retained; short-term availability improved.
3) Force-keep a small number of warm pods using a deployment with higher priorityClass to see if they survive competing allocations
   - Result: high-priority warm pods stayed around longer, but normal-priority pods were frequently preempted — created unfairness and potential capacity starvation for general traffic.

Hypotheses (rank-ordered):
A) Race between priming and eviction policies: the priming system requires sequential KV warm steps; if ordering is delayed (disk read, mmap latencies, or transient I/O), priming times out and autoscaler interprets repeated priming failures as node "bad" and removes it. This cycles into more cold start events.
B) Transient node-local disk pressure during model pulls causes readiness checks to fail, leading to eviction reasons that differ. Disk pressure might be from concurrent downloads + system logging + tiny ephemerals being written by model conversion steps.
C) Scheduler preemption thresholds are too coarse: when many short requests show up, kube-scheduler preempts warm pods aggressively to satisfy immediate pods, instead of routing to fallback models or throttling traffic.
D) Model artifact corruption or partial downloads cause loader to fail with mmap errors; the restart loop causes repeated warm attempts and churn. Not the only cause (does not explain disk pressure).

Things to surface to infra owners: 
- Audit autoscaler configuration for scaleDownUnneededTime, scaleDownUnreadyTime, and metrics used to decide node removal (are priming_failures counted as unready?).
- Add a separate metric that distinguishes "priming-in-progress" from "priming-failed" so scale-down rules can ignore in-progress warmups.
- Consider small reservation pool (2–4 GPUs) pinned to high-priority warm pods to act as warm-buffer (cheaper alternative than increasing global overprovision).

Immediate actionable checklist (short) :
- [ ] Reproduce in staging with synthetic load: 500 short requests + 20 long model loads to see if same cycles occur. (assigned: Priya)
- [ ] Add temporary debugging flags to serving-agent to log detailed mmap/download progress (Avery)
- [ ] Create dashboard panels for priming_attempts vs priming_success_rate vs node_scale_events (Diego)
- [ ] Open infra PR to increase scaleDownUnreadyTime to 10m in canary (PR linked above)

Notes on experiments: specific commands and things to capture when reproducing:
- Use locust/gatling to simulate request mix: 80% short (<=8 tokens), 20% long (>=512 tokens) targeting the dedicated pool route.
- Capture /tmp/serving-agent.dump on node when priming starts and when it times out.
- Instrument model pull path with timestamps: tar extraction start, open(mmap) call time, checksum verify time.

Open questions / TODO for followup:
- Is there a per-node daemon that throttles disk IO during boot or heavy downloads? (system config or cloud agent?)
- Do warp/quantize steps run concurrently on start and saturate CPU causing priming delays?
- Are we double-charging priming failures in both the scheduler and autoscaler decision-making?
- If we keep a small warm buffer, what is the expected cost delta and SLO improvement? (ask finance for rough estimate)

Raw traces & artifacts attached (links):
- See linked PR for config change attempt.
- Prometheus query snippets saved in the Jira ticket INF-2741.

Closing notes:
This felt like an orchestration-level feedback loop: warmups failing -> autoscaler punishes nodes -> fewer nodes -> more cold starts. Short-term mitigations (increase timeouts, longer scale-down delays, small priority pinned pool) help but still want to find root I/O or scheduling policy that flips the switch. Handing off to infra + scheduler owners to look at how priming state is surfaced to cluster autoscaler and whether eviction signals are too noisy.

If someone else is reading — add any ad-hoc tests you run here. Keep the chronology intact so next person can correlate timestamps against Prometheus and kube events.

End of notes.
